label: HDFS Fundamentals & Architecture
desc: 29 interview questions covering HDFS, Storage, Blocks, HDFS I/O and more.

subs.label: HDFS
subs.desc: HDFS is responsible for storing huge volumes of data across a cluster and is designed to run on commodity hardware.

subs.label: Storage
subs.desc: NAS (Network Attached Storage) — compute and storage are separated; storage is distributed over servers on a network.

subs.label: Blocks
subs.desc: In HDFS, data is split into blocks (typically 64MB or 128MB) distributed across the cluster, and each block is replicated multiple times (three, by default) across different nodes.

subs.label: HDFS I/O
subs.desc: Reading is done in parallel because it lets Hadoop access data faster — the whole point of distributing storage.

subs.label: Big Data
subs.desc: Traditional RDBMS is built for transactional systems — reporting and archiving data, and is useful when you want to look up a single record from a large data set.

subs.label: NameNode
subs.desc: Heartbeat — signals that the DataNode is still alive; the NameNode relies on periodic heartbeats to decide whether to keep using a DataNode.

subs.label: DataNode
subs.desc: When data is stored on a DataNode, the corresponding metadata is reported to the NameNode.

label: Replication, Rack Awareness & Fault Tolerance
desc: 15 interview questions covering Rack Awareness, Replication, Fault Tolerance.

subs.label: Rack Awareness
subs.desc: Most Hadoop components — NameNode, DataNode, and others — are "rack-aware," meaning they know which rack they're physically on.

subs.label: Replication
subs.desc: Replication factor is the number of copies of a file HDFS maintains.

subs.label: Fault Tolerance
subs.desc: A heartbeat is a signal indicating that a process is alive — a DataNode sends heartbeats to the NameNode, and a TaskTracker sends heartbeats to the JobTracker.

label: MapReduce Fundamentals
desc: 29 interview questions covering MapReduce, Data Locality, InputSplit, Blocks.

subs.label: MapReduce
subs.desc: Apache Hadoop is built on the MapReduce algorithm, in which Map and Reduce operations process very large data sets: the Map method filters and sorts data, and the Reduce method summarizes it — a concept borrowed from functional programming.

subs.label: Data Locality
subs.desc: Data locality means processing data wherever it already resides, rather than moving it — "moving computation is cheaper than moving data." This is only possible when the data is splittable, which it is by default.

subs.label: InputSplit
subs.desc: InputSplit is the chunk of data processed by a single mapper — in other words, the logical chunk of data assigned to one mapper.

subs.label: Blocks
subs.desc: What is the difference between block and split?

label: Mapper & Reducer Internals
desc: 19 interview questions covering Reducer, Mapper, MapReduce.

subs.label: Reducer
subs.desc: The main task of a Reducer is to reduce a larger set of data sharing a key down to a smaller set.

subs.label: Mapper
subs.desc: A ChainMapper is a special class that lets multiple mapper classes run in a chained fashion within a single map task — one mapper's output feeds directly into the next mapper's input, letting you chain any number of mappers together.

subs.label: MapReduce
subs.desc: How do you do value-level comparison?

label: Combiners, Partitioners & Shuffle
desc: 19 interview questions covering Partitioner, Combiner, Reducer.

subs.label: Partitioner
subs.desc: After the combiner and intermediate map output, the Partitioner controls the keys after sort and shuffle.

subs.label: Combiner
subs.desc: A Combiner is an optional class, specified via Job.setCombinerClass(ClassName), that performs local aggregation of intermediate outputs — cutting down the amount of data transferred from the Mapper to the Reducer.

subs.label: Reducer
subs.desc: The mapper's intermediate output is stored on the local file system (not HDFS) of each individual mapper node — typically a temporary directory location configured by the Hadoop administrator.

subs.label: JobTracker
subs.desc: JobTracker is a daemon service that submits and tracks MapReduce tasks across the Hadoop cluster.

subs.label: TaskTracker
subs.desc: A TaskTracker is a slave-node daemon that accepts tasks — Map, Reduce, and Shuffle operations — from a JobTracker.

label: Hadoop Ecosystem, Deployment & Configuration
desc: 27 interview questions covering Ecosystem, Cluster Hardware, Config, Hadoop Modes.

subs.label: Ecosystem
subs.desc: Hadoop provides DistCP (Distributed Copy), a MapReduce-based utility for large inter- or intra-cluster copies of data.

subs.label: Cluster Hardware
subs.desc: Commodity hardware is an inexpensive system that isn't high-quality or high-availability — Hadoop can run on any average commodity hardware and doesn't need supercomputers or high-end machines.

subs.label: Config
subs.desc: What are the default port numbers on which Nodes run in Hadoop? What are the important configuration files in Hadoop?

subs.label: Hadoop Modes
subs.desc: No Hadoop daemons run, and everything runs in a single Java process — so you don't get the benefit of distributing code across a cluster.

label: Performance, Tuning & Troubleshooting
desc: 19 interview questions covering Troubleshooting, Admin, Performance, Networking.

subs.label: Troubleshooting
subs.desc: Why do we use the fsck command in HDFS? Why might you get a connection-refused Java exception running Hadoop fsck?

subs.label: Admin
subs.desc: Similar to formatting a drive in Windows, formatting the DFS structures data properly — but it also formats the NameNode in the process, which is generally not something you want to do casually.

subs.label: Performance
subs.desc: Assuming a 64MB block size with 2 mappers and 2 reducers: 64 * 4 = 256MB of memory, and the OS needs at least 30% extra headroom, so 256 + 80 = 326MB of RAM is roughly required to process that chunk of data.

subs.label: Networking
subs.desc: SSH (Secure Shell) is a secure protocol and the most common way to administer remote servers safely — relatively simple and inexpensive to implement.
